s0003.literal: Xiong Tanlang; Zhou Di; Liu Yi; Chen Baoying
s0003.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang; Zhou Di; Liu Yi; Chen Baoying

s0004.literal: Xiong Tanlang was a native of Nanchang in Yuzhang; for generations his family was a leading clan of the commandery.
s0004.idiomatic: Xiong Tanlang came from Nanchang in Yuzhang; for generations his house had been a leading clan of the commandery.

s0005.literal: Tanlang was dissolute and unrestrained, possessed great physical strength, and had a very imposing appearance.
s0005.idiomatic: Tanlang was wild and ungoverned, powerfully built, and striking in looks.

s0006.literal: When the Hou Jing rebellion broke out, he gradually gathered young men, seized Fengcheng county as a palisade, and many fierce brigands and robbers joined him.
s0006.idiomatic: In the Hou Jing uprising he slowly gathered youths, took Fengcheng county for a stockade, and fierce raiders flocked to him.

s0007.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed him administrator of Bashan.
s0007.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang made him administrator of Bashan.

s0008.literal: When Jingzhou fell, Tanlang's military strength grew somewhat; he plundered neighboring counties, bound residents and sold them; among the mountain valleys he was the greatest scourge.
s0008.idiomatic: After Jingzhou fell his forces grew; he raided neighboring counties, bound commoners and sold them, and was the worst plague in the hills.

s0009.literal: When Hou Zhen garrisoned Yuzhang, Tanlang outwardly showed submission while secretly plotting against Zhen.
s0009.idiomatic: When Hou Zhen held Yuzhang, Tanlang feigned obedience while plotting against him in secret.

s0010.literal: When Hou Fang'er rebelled against Zhen, Tanlang was the chief plotter; when Zhen was defeated, Tanlang obtained a great many of Zhen's horses, weapons, women, and children.
s0010.idiomatic: When Hou Fang'er turned on Zhen, Tanlang masterminded it; after Zhen's defeat Tanlang took a great haul of horses, arms, women, and children.

s0011.literal: When Xiao Bo crossed the mountains, Ouyang Yi served as vanguard; Tanlang deceived Yi into joining him on an expedition to Bashan to strike Huang Fading, while also notifying Fading of a joint appointment to break Yi, agreeing, "When the affair succeeds, give me horses and arms."
s0011.idiomatic: When Xiao Bo crossed the range, Ouyang Yi led the van; Tanlang tricked Yi into a joint strike on Huang Fading in Bashan while telling Fading they would crush Yi together, with the bargain, "If we win, the horses and gear are mine."

s0012.literal: When the army marched out, it advanced pincer-wise with Yi; Tanlang again deceived Yi, saying, "Yu Xiaoding intends to ambush you—we must leave a striking force; with so few arms and armor, I fear we cannot succeed."
s0012.idiomatic: On campaign he moved in concert with Yi, then lied again: "Yu Xiaoding means to ambush you—we must keep a hidden reserve; with so little armor I fear we cannot manage."

s0013.literal: Yi then sent three hundred suits of armor to assist him.
s0013.idiomatic: Yi sent three hundred suits of armor to help.

s0014.literal: When they reached the city and were about to fight, Tanlang feigned retreat; Fading pressed the pursuit; Yi lost support and withdrew in disarray; Tanlang took his horses and arms and returned.
s0014.idiomatic: At the walls, about to engage, Tanlang pretended flight; Fading pressed in; Yi lost his support and broke in disorder; Tanlang seized the horses and arms and went home.

s0015.literal: At the time Chen Ding of Bashan also held troops and built a stockade; Tanlang falsely offered his daughter to Ding's son in marriage.
s0015.idiomatic: Chen Ding of Bashan also held men in a fort; Tanlang falsely offered his daughter to Ding's son.

s0016.literal: He also said to Ding, "Zhou Di and Yu Xiaoding both do not wish this marriage—you must send a strong force to welcome the bride."
s0016.idiomatic: He told Ding, "Zhou Di and Yu Xiaoding both oppose this match—you must send a strong escort to fetch the bride."

s0017.literal: Ding then dispatched three hundred picked troops together with twenty local strongmen to welcome her; when they arrived, Tanlang seized them, collected their horses and arms, and set a price for ransom.
s0017.idiomatic: Ding sent three hundred elite troops and twenty local magnates to escort her; when they came Tanlang seized them, took horse and gear, and set a ransom.

s0018.literal: In Shaotai year 2, as a southern-river magnate Tanlang was by precedent made roaming-cavalry general.
s0018.idiomatic: In Shaotai year 2 (550), as a southern-river strongman he was made roaming-cavalry general by precedent.

s0019.literal: Soon he was made credential-bearing, fierce-whirlwind general with acting staff as inspector of Gui prefecture, concurrently magistrate of Fengcheng, and served in succession as administrators of Yixin and Yuzhang commanderies.
s0019.idiomatic: Soon he received the credential staff, was made fierce-whirlwind general with acting authority as inspector of Gui, held Fengcheng as magistrate, and in turn governed Yixin and Yuzhang.

s0020.literal: Wang Lin sent Li Xiaoqin and others with Yu Xiaoding to attack Zhou Di at Linchuan; Tanlang led his forces to aid them.
s0020.idiomatic: Wang Lin sent Li Xiaoqin and others with Yu Xiaoding to strike Zhou Di at Linchuan; Tanlang marched to their aid.

s0021.literal: That year, for merit he was made credential-bearing, regular attendant of the fast track, pacifying-the-distance general, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yonghua with a fief of one thousand households, and granted one set of pipes and drums.
s0021.idiomatic: That year, for merit, he was made credential-bearing fast-track regular attendant and pacifying-the-distance general, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yonghua with a thousand-household fief, and given pipes and drums.

s0022.literal: For merit in resisting Wang Lin he was further made pacifying-the-west general and opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes; the rest remained as before.
s0022.idiomatic: For resisting Wang Lin he was further made pacifying-the-west general and opener equal to the three dukes; other posts stood unchanged.

s0023.literal: When Zhou Wenyu attacked Yu Xiaomou at Yuzhang, Tanlang marched out to join him; Wenyu was defeated and Tanlang then killed Wenyu to join Wang Lin—the affair is told in Wenyu's biography.
s0023.idiomatic: When Zhou Wenyu attacked Yu Xiaomou at Yuzhang, Tanlang came out to join him; Wenyu lost, and Tanlang killed Wenyu to answer Wang Lin—as told in Wenyu's biography.

s0024.literal: Thereupon he seized all of Wenyu's subordinate generals, held Xingan county, and walled the river bank as his city.
s0024.idiomatic: He then seized all Wenyu's generals, held Xingan county, and walled the river line for a city.

s0025.literal: When Wang Lin marched east, Emperor Wen summoned southern-river troops; Zhou Di, inspector of Jiang, and Huang Fading, inspector of Gao, wished to follow the stream to answer the call; Tanlang then held the city and arrayed ships to block them; Di and the others with Fading therefore led southern troops to build walls and besiege him, cutting off his messengers with Lin.
s0025.idiomatic: When Wang Lin went east, Emperor Wen called up the southern rivers; Zhou Di of Jiang and Huang Fading of Gao meant to sail downstream to answer; Tanlang held the city and lined ships to block them; Di and Fading then led southern troops to wall and besiege him, severing his couriers to Lin.

s0026.literal: When Wang Lin was defeated and fled, Tanlang's party and allies lost heart; Di stormed the city, capturing men and women numbering more than ten thousand.
s0026.idiomatic: When Wang Lin was broken and fled, Tanlang's allies lost heart; Di stormed the city and took more than ten thousand men and women.

s0027.literal: Tanlang fled into a village; villagers beheaded him; his head was sent to the capital and hung at the Vermilion Bird Observatory.
s0027.idiomatic: Tanlang fled into a hamlet; villagers cut off his head; it was sent to the capital and hung at the Vermilion Bird Observatory.

s0028.literal: Editorial footnote marker 1. Thereupon his entire clan was seized; none, young or old, escaped public execution.
s0028.idiomatic: [1] His whole clan was then seized; young and old alike were executed in the market.

s0029.literal: Zhou Di was a native of Nancheng in Linchuan.
s0029.idiomatic: Zhou Di came from Nancheng in Linchuan.

s0030.literal: In youth he lived in the mountain valleys, possessed great strength, could draw powerful crossbows, and made his living by hunting with bow.
s0030.idiomatic: As a youth he lived in the hills, was powerfully built, could draw heavy crossbows, and lived by the hunt.

s0031.literal: When the Hou Jing rebellion broke out, Di's clansman Zhou Xu raised troops in Linchuan; the Prince of Shixing of Liang, Xiao Yi, yielded the commandery to Xu; Di recruited fellow townsmen to follow him, and in every battle his courage topped all the armies.
s0031.idiomatic: In the Hou Jing turmoil Di's kinsman Zhou Xu raised men in Linchuan; Liang's Prince of Shixing, Xiao Yi, yielded the commandery to Xu; Di gathered neighbors to follow, and in every fight his courage led the host.

s0032.literal: The commanders under Xu were all leading families of the commandery and gradually grew arrogant; Xu restrained them somewhat, and the commanders all resented it; they therefore joined to kill Xu and made Di their leader; Di then held the territory of Linchuan and built a city at Gongtang.
s0032.idiomatic: Xu's subordinate chiefs were all commandery magnates and grew proud; Xu checked them, and they turned resentful, killed Xu together, and set up Di; Di then held Linchuan and walled Gongtang.

s0033.literal: Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed Di credential-bearing, regular attendant of the fast track, stalwart martial general, and inspector of Gao prefecture, enfeoffing him as Marquis of Linru with a fief of five hundred households.
s0033.idiomatic: Emperor Yuan of Liang made Di credential-bearing fast-track regular attendant and stalwart-martial general, inspector of Gao, and Marquis of Linru with five hundred households.

s0034.literal: In Shaotai year 2 he was made interior administrator of Linchuan.
s0034.idiomatic: In Shaotai year 2 (550) he was made interior administrator of Linchuan.

s0035.literal: Soon he was granted envoy's credential staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, trustworthy-prestige general, and inspector of Heng prefecture, while still holding the interior administration of Linchuan.
s0035.idiomatic: Soon he received envoy credentials, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, trustworthy-prestige general, and the inspectorship of Heng while still governing Linchuan within.

s0036.literal: When Zhou Wenyu campaigned against Xiao Bo, Di held his troops and guarded his borders, watching how the struggle would end.
s0036.idiomatic: When Zhou Wenyu attacked Xiao Bo, Di kept his men in camp and guarded his borders, watching the outcome.

s0037.literal: Wenyu sent his chief clerk Lu Shan'cai to persuade Di; Di then brought out grain and supplies in great quantity to supply Wenyu.
s0037.idiomatic: Wenyu sent chief clerk Lu Shan'cai to win Di over; Di then poured out grain and stores to feed Wenyu's army.

s0038.literal: When Bo was pacified, for merit he was promoted to quelling-the-distance general and transferred to inspector of Jiang prefecture.
s0038.idiomatic: When Bo was pacified, for merit he was raised to quelling-the-distance general and made inspector of Jiang.

s0039.literal: When the Founder received the abdication and Wang Lin marched east, Di wished to hold the southern rivers for himself; he therefore summoned the administrators of eight commanderies under him to swear alliance, claiming he would enter to answer the call; the court feared he would turn rebel and therefore treated him with rich consolation.
s0039.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne and Wang Lin went east, Di meant to keep the southern rivers; he called the eight commandery heads to swear alliance, saying he would march to answer the summons; the court feared revolt and soothed him generously.

s0040.literal: When Lin reached Poyang, Yu Xiaoding, lord of the Xinwu cave settlement, raised troops to answer Lin.
s0040.idiomatic: At Poyang, Xinwu cave lord Yu Xiaoding rose for Lin.

s0041.literal: Lin thought the southern-river commanderies could be settled by proclamation alone and therefore sent his generals Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and others south to gather grain.
s0041.idiomatic: Lin judged the southern commanderies would fall to a proclamation and sent Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and others south for grain.

s0042.literal: Meng and the others joined Yu Xiaoding; their forces were nearly twenty thousand; they came pressing on Gongtang, linking eight forts to corner Di.
s0042.idiomatic: Meng joined Yu Xiaoding; together they neared twenty thousand men and pressed Gongtang, chaining eight forts against Di.

s0043.literal: Di sent Zhou Fu to lead troops and encamp at the old seat of Linchuan commandery, cutting off the river mouth; he then came out to fight, routed them utterly, slaughtered the eight forts, and sent Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and Yu Xiaoding alive to the capital; he collected their military stores—arms piled like hills—and also captured their men and horses, which Di kept for himself.
s0043.idiomatic: Di sent Zhou Fu to hold the old Linchuan seat and choke the river mouth, then sallied and crushed them, razed the eight forts, and sent Li Xiaoqin, Fan Meng, and Yu Xiaoding alive to court; arms and stores heaped like hills—and men and horses Di kept.

s0044.literal: In Yongding year 2, for merit he was promoted to pacifying-the-south general and opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes; his fief was increased by one thousand five hundred households, and he was granted one set of pipes and drums.
s0044.idiomatic: In Yongding year 2 (558), for merit he was made pacifying-the-south general and opener equal to the three dukes, with fifteen hundred more households and pipes and drums.

s0045.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, Di's title was advanced to pacifying-the-south general.
s0045.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne, Di was advanced to pacifying-the-south general.

s0046.literal: Editorial footnote marker 2. When Xiong Tanlang rebelled, Di with Zhou Fu, Huang Fading, and others led troops together to besiege Tanlang, slaughtered him, and wholly took over his following.
s0046.idiomatic: [2] When Xiong Tanlang rebelled, Di with Zhou Fu and Huang Fading jointly besieged him, destroyed him, and absorbed all his men.

s0047.literal: After Wang Lin was defeated, Emperor Wen summoned Di to go out and garrison Poyang and also summoned his son to court; Di hesitated and looked back and forth, and neither came.
s0047.idiomatic: After Wang Lin's defeat, Emperor Wen called Di to garrison Poyang and his son to court; Di wavered and would not come—neither of them.

s0048.literal: The administrator of Yuzhang, Zhou Fu, had originally been subordinate to Di; at this time he with Huang Fading led their commands to the capital; Emperor Wen recorded their merit in breaking Xiong Tanlang and both added rank and reward; when Di heard it he was very resentful and therefore secretly joined with Liu Yi.
s0048.idiomatic: Yuzhang administrator Zhou Fu had once served Di; now he and Huang Fading brought their troops to court; Emperor Wen credited their part in breaking Tanlang and heaped honors on them; Di, hearing it, burned with resentment and secretly allied with Liu Yi.

s0049.literal: When the imperial army campaigned against Yi, Di in suspicion and fear could not be at ease; he therefore sent his younger brother Fangxing to lead troops and strike Zhou Fu; Fu fought and defeated him.
s0049.idiomatic: When the court moved on Liu Yi, Di, uneasy with fear, sent his brother Fangxing against Zhou Fu; Fu met him and broke him.

s0050.literal: He also separately sent troops to strike Hua Jiao at Poyang; the affair was discovered and they were all seized by Jiao.
s0050.idiomatic: He also sent another force against Hua Jiao at Poyang; the plot came out and Jiao seized them all.

s0051.literal: Collation variant: (Tianjia). In the third year, spring, Editorial footnote marker 3. Emperor Wen then issued an edict pardoning the southern-river gentry and commoners misled by Di, and ordered Wu Mingche, inspector of Jiang, to command all armies together with Huang Fading, inspector of Gao, and Zhou Fu, administrator of Yuzhang, to campaign against Di.
s0051.idiomatic: Collation variant: (Tianjia). In spring of the third year, [3] Emperor Wen pardoned southern-river people led astray by Di and ordered Jiang inspector Wu Mingche to command all forces with Gao inspector Huang Fading and Yuzhang administrator Zhou Fu against Di.

s0052.literal: Thereupon the Masters of Writing issued a warrant, saying:
s0052.idiomatic: The Masters of Writing then issued a warrant, saying:

s0053.literal: To the gentry and commoners of Linchuan commandery: In ancient times the Western Capital flourished, yet Xin and Yue turned disloyal;
s0053.idiomatic: To the people of Linchuan: In old days the Western Capital stood in glory, yet Xin and Yue turned traitor;

s0054.literal: when the Eastern Capital revived, Yin and Chong defied allegiance.
s0054.idiomatic: when the Eastern Capital rose again, Yin and Chong broke faith.

s0055.literal: Therefore hawk and eagle contend in pursuit, and punishments of mincing extend to execution—since antiquity this has existed, and its origins are very old.
s0055.idiomatic: So hawk and eagle hunt one another, and the extreme penalty of mincing has been known from of old—its roots run deep.

s0056.literal: The rebel Zhou Di was originally of low station; in Liang's time of ruin he ravaged the mountain valleys.
s0056.idiomatic: The rebel Zhou Di sprang from humble ranks; in Liang's collapse he plundered the hills.

s0057.literal: Our Founder personally led the hundred Yue, halted his army at the nine rivers, washed away their mud and sand and lent them feather and down, cut the pig tally and apportioned the beast seal—Editorial footnote marker 4.—fostering kindness such as no other equals.
s0057.idiomatic: Our Founder himself led the hundred Yue, halted at the nine rivers, washed mud from them and lent them feather and down, cut the pig tally and split the beast seal—[4]—a brooding kindness none could match.

s0058.literal: When the imperial fortune first took root, he broadly showed good faith, yet amid the state's hard straits he scarcely rendered service.
s0058.idiomatic: When the dynasty's fortune began he showed good faith, yet in the state's distress he barely served.

s0059.literal: With dragon tally and embroidered robe he borrowed royal rank to rule those below; with bear banner and linked armor he relied on rugged ground to look down on his superiors.
s0059.idiomatic: Dragon tally and embroidered robe let him rule from borrowed rank; bear banner and mail let him tower from rugged ground over his betters.

s0060.literal: When Wang Lin first turned disloyal and Xiao Bo was not yet pacified, he joined the three Xiang in the west and the five ranges in the south; when Heng and Guang were settled and the rebellious were calmed, the Jiang and Ying regions were again in turmoil and treachery rose anew—he held a single commandery, clinging to a hundred shifting hearts, his intent and bearing always at odds, his words and tracks never matching.
s0060.idiomatic: When Wang Lin first wavered and Xiao Bo still stood, he tied to the three Xiang westward and the five ranges southward; Heng and Guang were quieted and rebels steadied, yet Jiang and Ying stirred again—he clutched one commandery with a hundred fickle hearts, face and deed ever at odds, word and trail never aligned.

s0061.literal: Only because Xinwu was not yet settled and the land was remote with strong troops did mutual swallowing make his power.
s0061.idiomatic: Only while Xinwu stayed unsettled and distant ground bred strong arms did mutual swallowing build his strength.

s0062.literal: He collected arms and gear and captured gentry and commoners, calling them all private property, and never once reported victory.
s0062.idiomatic: Arms he gathered, people he seized, and called it all private spoil—never once reporting victory to the throne.

s0063.literal: When the court sent a single envoy, he always held to two sides.
s0063.idiomatic: When the court sent one envoy, he still straddled both sides.

s0064.literal: The court in its vast forbearance drew him in with high honor; he then stood equal to the Three Hushes and shared duty with the Four Peaks—wealth and rank towering, surpassing all meritorious servants.
s0064.idiomatic: The court, broad in mercy, drew him close with honor until he ranked with the Three Hushes and shared the Four Peaks' burden—wealth and title towering above every merit-holder.

s0065.literal: Moreover, when armies crossed the ranges he answered from afar; he held his troops and blocked the river, then suddenly turned suspicious and defiant.
s0065.idiomatic: When armies crossed the hills he answered from afar; he held his men and barred the river, then turned sudden and defiant.

s0066.literal: The late Minister of Works, the Lamented Duke, treated him as kin by clan pact, close as flesh and bone; their walled cities adjoined, their strength like lips and teeth; yet at the disaster of Pengwang he sat and watched difficulty arise—on that grievance he bound his faction.
s0066.idiomatic: The late lamented Minister of Works treated him as sworn kin, bone to bone; their walls touched, strength like lips and teeth—yet at Pengwang's ruin he only watched trouble grow, and on that grudge knit his faction.

s0067.literal: At that time northern invaders pressed the borders and western rebels leaned on the land; sandals and grain he wholly supplied to the enemy; rank and military display he wholly followed the false party.
s0067.idiomatic: Northern raiders then pressed the frontier and western rebels leaned on the land; sandals and grain he fed the foe; rank and martial show he copied the rebel host.

s0068.literal: When the imperial army returned in triumph and greatly settled the realm, the heavenly net was broad and cast him beyond its mesh; with imperial writs and edicts the court soothed him again and again; caps and girdles of office-holders were heaped upon him in layers.
s0068.idiomatic: When the imperial host returned victorious and the realm was largely settled, heaven's net was wide and set him outside it—yet edict on edict soothed him, honors on honors from the girdled ranks.

s0069.literal: As for the slaughter of Xiong Tanlang and the taking of Fengcheng, that was chiefly the founding merit of Equal-in-Honor Fading and the exertion of pacifying-the-west Zhou Fu; the Ministry of Awards has its canon and rich reward is the old rule—yet he hated the upright and loathed the true, making himself their enemy; against ritual and in secret plot he therefore grew worse.
s0069.idiomatic: The fall of Xiong Tanlang and Fengcheng came chiefly from Fading's founding merit and Fu's exertion—the Ministry of Awards keeps its rule and rich reward is ancient custom—yet he hated the upright, made enemies of the true, and against ritual and in secret plot grew worse still.

s0070.literal: Summoned to leave Poyang, for years he would not come; asked to send a son to attend court, for years the boy did not present himself.
s0070.idiomatic: Called from Poyang, he would not come for years; asked for a son at court, the boy stayed away for years.

s0071.literal: Outwardly he lured fugitives and gathered the ungoverned; inwardly he stirred the capital, scheming for the extraordinary.
s0071.idiomatic: Outside he lured fugitives and gathered rowdies; inside he stirred the capital, scheming the unthinkable.

s0072.literal: He levied taxes on his own authority and rarely sent revenue to the nine treasuries; he blocked the two merchant routes and harmed the four classes of people.
s0072.idiomatic: He taxed on his own and seldom sent coin to the nine treasuries; he choked the two trade roads and hurt the four orders of folk.

s0073.literal: He secretly joined the rebel Yi, inside and outside as one garment; seeking the same evil, they aided each other in secret.
s0073.idiomatic: He secretly joined rebel Liu Yi, outer and inner as one coat; alike in evil, they answered each other in secret.

s0074.literal: He thought our six armies' shallow campaign and the three Yue not yet settled—when we slaughtered and broke Shucheng, bound wives and children, and separately struck the Poyang garrison, he raised arms in the Li country, coerced tribal chiefs, and besieged walled cities; fortunate that the state was prepared, he was beaten and destroyed at once.
s0074.idiomatic: He judged our six hosts' light campaign and the three Yue still restless—yet when we broke Shucheng, seized wives and children, and struck Poyang apart, he raised arms in the Li lands, coerced chiefs, and besieged towns; the state was ready, and he was crushed at once.

s0075.literal: Acting on credential, fast-track regular attendant, humane-martial general, and administrator of Xunyang, Marquis of Huairen, Hua Jiao, and bright-prestige general, administrator of Luling, Viscount of Yiyang, Lu Zilong, both broke the rebel bands and recovered their commandery territories whole.
s0075.idiomatic: Acting-credential fast-track regular attendant, humane-martial general, Xunyang administrator, Marquis of Huairen Hua Jiao, and bright-prestige general, Luling administrator, Viscount of Yiyang Lu Zilong, both broke the rebels and restored their commanderies entire.

s0076.literal: Credential-bearing, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-west general, inspector of Ding prefecture, Editorial footnote marker 5. concurrently administrator of Yuzhang, Marquis of Xifeng, Zhou Fu, himself defended the ditch and rampart and took the arrows and stones; leading these loyal and brave men, with few he crushed many—heads and ears by the tens of thousands, captives by the thousands.
s0076.idiomatic: Credential-bearing scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-west general, Ding inspector, [5] and Yuzhang administrator, Marquis of Xifeng Zhou Fu, manned ditch and wall and stood in the arrow storm; with loyal courage and few men he broke many—tens of thousands slain, thousands taken.

s0077.literal: Di was then gathering the last embers and returning to hold the walls and towers.
s0077.idiomatic: Di was gathering embers and clinging again to wall and tower.

s0078.literal: Envoy-credential, pacifying-the-south general, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, inspector of Gao prefecture, Marquis of Xinjian, Fading, had long shown heroic achievement and from of old stood in loyalty; before he received the royal command he had led loyal troops of his own; he both aided Fu and the others and wholly saved Zilong; wrapping grain and donning armor he still pursued the flying foe; troops that beat the bear ran faster than lightning; warriors who shook mountains shouted and moved peaks—with such pursuit none should remain.
s0078.idiomatic: Envoy-credential pacifying-the-south general, opener equal to the three dukes, Gao inspector, Marquis of Xinjian Fading, had shown heroism early and loyalty long; before royal orders he led loyal troops, aided Fu, and saved Zilong whole—grain wrapped, armor on, still chasing the flying foe; bear-beating hosts outran lightning; mountain-shaking warriors shouted hills aside—by such pursuit none should escape.

s0079.literal: Though a rotten stump is about to fall and needs no second axe, and fallen leaves are about to perish and need no fierce wind;
s0079.idiomatic: Though a rotten stump will fall without a second axe, and fallen leaves will die without a gale wind;

s0080.literal: yet to uproot weeds one must act before they spread, and to stamp out fire one must value quick extinction; dividing orders among generals truly relies on heroic decisiveness.
s0080.idiomatic: yet weeds are uprooted before they spread, and fire is quenched while the blaze is small—orders divided among generals truly need heroic fruit.

s0081.literal: Now we send the pacifying-the-south equal-in-honor's marshal of the army, Xiangdong Duke's chancellor Liu Guangde, together with pacifying-the-west marshal Sun Xiao, administrator of North Xin'ai Lu Guangda, credential-bearing pacifying-the-south general, inspector of Wu prefecture, Marquis of Pengze Lu Xida, with ten thousand armored men, marching out from Xingkou.
s0081.idiomatic: We now send pacifying-the-south equal-in-honor's army marshal, Xiangdong duke's chancellor Liu Guangde, with pacifying-the-west marshal Sun Xiao, North Xin'ai administrator Lu Guangda, credential-bearing pacifying-the-south general and Wu inspector Marquis of Pengze Lu Xida, and ten thousand armored men, marching from Xingkou.

s0082.literal: We also send the former administrator of Wu Xing, Hu Shuo, the merit-establishing general and former administrator of Xuancheng Qian Facheng, the administrators of Tianmen and Yiyang, Fan Yi, the cloud-banner general and inspector of He prefecture, Marquis of Nangu, Jiao Sengdu, the stern-martial general and inspector of Jian prefecture, Viscount of Chen, Zhang Zhida, and credential-bearing commander of Jiang and Wu regions, pacifying-the-south general, inspector of Jiang prefecture, Marquis of Anwu, Wu Mingche, with tower ships, horse, and foot, pointing straight at Linchuan.
s0082.idiomatic: We also send former Wu Xing administrator Hu Shuo, merit-establishing general and former Xuancheng administrator Qian Facheng, Tianmen and Yiyang administrators Fan Yi, cloud-banner general and He inspector Marquis of Nangu Jiao Sengdu, stern-martial general and Jian inspector Viscount of Chen Zhang Zhida, and credential-bearing commander of Jiang and Wu, pacifying-the-south general, Jiang inspector Marquis of Anwu Wu Mingche, with tower ships and horse and foot straight at Linchuan.

s0083.literal: The former interior administrator of Ancheng, Liu Shijing, the administrator of Bashan, Cai Senggui, the interior administrator of Nankang, Liu Feng, the administrator of Luling, Lu Zilong, and the interior administrator of Ancheng, Que Shen, all receive Fading's command and will assemble at the old commandery seat.
s0083.idiomatic: Former Ancheng interior administrator Liu Shijing, Bashan administrator Cai Senggui, Nankang interior administrator Liu Feng, Luling administrator Lu Zilong, and Ancheng interior administrator Que Shen all take Fading's orders and meet at the old commandery seat.

s0084.literal: We also order the administrator of Xunyang, Hua Jiao, the bright-blaze general and administrator of Ba prefecture, Pan Chuntuo, the pacifying-the-west general and inspector of Ying prefecture, Marquis of Xinle, Zhang Zhaoda, all to lead tiger hosts and go straight to the rebel city.
s0084.idiomatic: We also order Xunyang administrator Hua Jiao, bright-blaze general and Ba administrator Pan Chuntuo, and pacifying-the-west general and Ying inspector Marquis of Xinle Zhang Zhaoda, each leading tiger troops straight to the rebel city.

s0085.literal: Envoy-credential, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-south general, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, inspector of Xiang prefecture, Duke of Xiangdong commandery, Du, dispatches wing commanders in succession on the road; war boats cover the water and armored horsemen fill the hills.
s0085.idiomatic: Envoy-credential scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-south general, opener equal to the three dukes, Xiang inspector, Duke of Xiangdong Du, sends wing after wing on the road—war boats blanket the water, armored riders the hills.

s0086.literal: We also command pacifying-the-south general and opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes Ouyang Yi to lead his sons—the inspector of Jiao prefecture Sheng, the newly appointed right leader of the crown prince's guard Sui, the inspector of Heng prefecture Hou Xiao, and others—Editorial footnote marker 6.—with strong Yue troops to cross the ranges northward.
s0086.idiomatic: We also command pacifying-the-south general and opener equal to the three dukes Ouyang Yi to lead his sons—Jiao inspector Sheng, the newly made crown-prince right leader Sui, Heng inspector Hou Xiao, and others—[6]—with hard Yue troops over the ranges north.

s0087.literal: A thousand li on the same schedule, a hundred roads all gathering—if we delay execution even another ten days and half a month, the Minister of Works, grand commander, will already have pacified the rebel Yi and returned in triumph not long after; when the drinking ceremony is complete we shall drive the victory in a long pursuit and stamp out the vicious, like singeing hair.
s0087.idiomatic: A thousand li on one timetable, a hundred roads converging—if we linger on punishment another fortnight, the Minister of Works and grand commander will already have pacified Liu Yi and soon return victorious; when the drinking rite ends we drive the victory straight on and stamp the vicious out like singeing hair.

s0088.literal: There is already a clear edict: guilt rests on Di alone; what crime have the people? All are pardoned.
s0088.idiomatic: A clear edict already states: guilt is Di's alone; what fault have the people? All are forgiven.

s0089.literal: Whoever by the occasion establishes merit will be rewarded according to a separate statute;
s0089.idiomatic: Whoever seizes the moment for merit will be rewarded by separate statute;

s0090.literal: whoever clings to error and does not change, punishment knows no pardon.
s0090.idiomatic: whoever clings to error unchanged, the law knows no mercy.

s0091.literal: When Wu Mingche reached Linchuan he ordered the armies to build linked walls to attack Di; they faced each other and could not overcome him; Emperor Wen then sent Emperor Gaozong to take overall command of the campaign; Di's host collapsed; wives and children were all seized; he alone slipped away over the ranges to Jin'an and relied on Chen Baoying.
s0091.idiomatic: Wu Mingche reached Linchuan and ordered linked siegeworks against Di; they faced each other without victory; Emperor Wen then sent Emperor Gaozong to command the campaign overall; Di's men collapsed, wife and children all taken; he alone fled over the ranges to Jin'an and clung to Chen Baoying.

s0092.literal: Baoying supplied Di with troops and stores; Liu Yi also sent his second son, the Loyal Subject, to follow him.
s0092.idiomatic: Baoying armed Di with troops and stores; Liu Yi also sent his second son, the Loyal Subject, to follow.

s0093.literal: The next autumn he again crossed the Dongxing range; the people of Dongxing, Nancheng, and Yongcheng counties were all Di's old associates and again answered him together.
s0093.idiomatic: Next autumn he crossed Dongxing Pass again; people of Dongxing, Nancheng, and Yongcheng were all his old ties and rose for him once more.

s0094.literal: Emperor Wen sent the commander Zhang Zhaoda to campaign against Di; Di again scattered into the mountain valleys.
s0094.idiomatic: Emperor Wen sent commander Zhang Zhaoda against Di; Di again melted into the hills.

s0095.literal: Earlier, when the Hou Jing rebellion broke out, the common people all abandoned their proper occupations and gathered as bandits; only in the territory under Di's rule was there no plundering; he even divided fields among them, supervised their farming, and the people pursued their trades—each had surplus stores; his government and teaching were strict and clear, and levies always arrived; commanderies that lacked supplies all looked to him for relief.
s0095.idiomatic: In the Hou Jing turmoil commoners had abandoned their trades and banded as robbers; only under Di was there no looting—he parceled fields, oversaw farming, and folk worked their trades with surplus in every storehouse; rule was strict, levies sure, and needy commanderies lived on his grain.

s0096.literal: Di's nature was plain and simple; he did not attend to ceremonial display; in winter he wore a short cloth robe, in summer a purple-gauze belly-wrap; in daily life he went barefoot; though outwardly he arrayed guards and soldiers, inwardly he had female performers; twisting rope and splitting bamboo, he was as if no one were present.
s0096.idiomatic: Di was plain by nature and cared nothing for display; in winter a short cloth coat, in summer a purple gauze belly-wrap; usually barefoot; though guards stood without, singers within, he twisted rope and split bamboo as if alone.

s0097.literal: Yet he was light with wealth and fond of giving; in all he aided, even the smallest measure was weighed with a balance; he was slow of speech yet his breast was faithful and true—the people of Linchuan all blessed him.
s0097.idiomatic: Yet he was free with wealth and loved to give; every gift he weighed to the hair; slow of tongue but faithful in heart—the people of Linchuan all honored him.

s0098.literal: At this time they all hid him together; though punishments were heaped on them, none would speak.
s0098.idiomatic: Now they hid him together; though execution pressed them, none would tell.

s0099.literal: Zhaoda then crossed the range and encamped at Jian'an, resisting Chen Baoying; Di again gathered his forces and came out at Dongxing.
s0099.idiomatic: Zhaoda crossed the pass and camped at Jian'an against Chen Baoying; Di gathered men again and came out at Dongxing.

s0100.literal: At the time Qian Su, administrator of Xuancheng, garrisoned Dongxing and yielded the city to Di.
s0100.idiomatic: Xuancheng administrator Qian Su then held Dongxing and surrendered the city to Di.
